summary.text: Lesson 2-6 of enVision Math Grade 4: the subtraction algorithm on greater numbers — borrow chains through zeros, the inverse-operation check, scouting regroups in advance, and estimates as the guard rail.

why.text: Big subtractions are where quiet errors thrive: a flipped column or a lost borrow looks fine on the page. The two habits taught here — scout the columns, run the addition check — are what make five-digit answers trustworthy.

objectives.text: Subtract numbers through six digits with regrouping
Check a subtraction with the inverse addition
Solve backwards for a missing starting number
Predict where the regroups will happen before working

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-6. The two-alarm habit is the theme: estimate before, addition-check after. One question makes her act on a FAILED check — that is deliberate; knowing what to do when the alarm rings matters more than the alarm. Borrow chains through zeros appear here gently and become the whole of lesson 2-7.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Scout each subtraction's columns before working it.

cards.def:
**More columns, same trades — the subtraction algorithm scales without changing.**
• 34,287 − 21,893 runs exactly like 534 − 278, five columns wide.
• Slow is fine. Every column is its own small problem.

**Addition and subtraction undo each other — which turns every answer into a checkable claim.**
• 34,287 − 21,893 = 12,394, because 12,394 + 21,893 = 34,287.
• With five-digit numbers the check earns its keep: more columns, more places to slip.

**Before subtracting, scan each column: anywhere the top digit is smaller, a trade is coming.**
• In 82,354 − 47,182: the tens (5 under 8) and the thousands (2 under 7) will both borrow.
• Knowing where the trades live turns the algorithm from a surprise into a plan.
cards.hint: Read the columns before you work them, like reading the road before you drive it.

cards.def:
**Round both numbers, subtract the rounds, and keep that number in view.**
• 34,287 − 21,893: about 34,000 − 22,000 = 12,000.
• An exact answer thousands away from the estimate does not get the benefit of the doubt.

questions.q: A national park logs 34,287 visitors in July and 21,893 in August. How many more visited in July?
steps: Ones: 7 − 3 = 4. Tens: 8 − 9 cannot go — trade: 18 − 9 = 9.
Hundreds: after lending, 1 − 8 cannot go — trade: 11 − 8 = 3.
Thousands: after lending, 3 − 1 = 2. Ten thousands: 3 − 2 = 1.
Difference: 12,394 — right beside the 12,000 estimate.

ex.main: **12,394.** Two mid-number trades, and the estimate vouches for the result.
ex.tip: Check: 12,394 + 21,893 = 34,287. With this many columns, the check is not optional politeness.

questions.hint: Only one column needs a trade.
steps: Ones: 0 − 0 = 0. Tens: 5 − 8 cannot go — trade: 15 − 8 = 7.
Hundreds: after lending, 3 − 1 = 2. Thousands: 6 − 2 = 4.
Ten thousands: 7 − 3 = 4. Difference: 44,270.

ex.main: **44,270.** One trade in the tens; everything else subtracts cleanly.
ex.tip: Not every big subtraction is a regrouping storm. Scout the columns first and you will know what is coming.

questions.q: Which estimate belongs beside the exact work for 34,287 − 21,893?
questions.hint: Round each number to the nearest thousand on its own digit.
steps: 34,287: the 2 in the hundreds keeps it at 34,000.
21,893: the 8 in the hundreds pushes it to 22,000.

ex.main: **12,000.** Each number rounded on its own digit — 21,893 goes up, not down.
ex.tip: Misrounding 21,893 to 21,000 is the tempting error: the 8 in its hundreds place says up.

questions.hint: Almost every column borrows — take them one at a time.
steps: Ones: 6 − 7 needs a borrow, but the tens hold 0 — the ripple runs left to the 3 hundreds.
After the ripple the top reads 2 hundreds, 9 tens, 16 ones. Ones: 16 − 7 = 9. Tens: 9 − 1 = 8.
Hundreds: 2 − 4 borrows from the thousands: 12 − 4 = 8. Thousands: 1 − 8 borrows again: 11 − 8 = 3. Ten thousands: 4 − 2 = 2.

ex.main: **23,889.** A borrow chain ran through the zero — the check is what makes the answer trustworthy.
ex.tip: When a borrow passes through a 0, the 0 becomes 9 and passes the request left. That chain is 2-7's whole subject.

steps: The subtraction claims 45,162 splits into 18,725 and 26,437.
Reassemble: 26,437 + 18,725.
It lands on 45,162 exactly — claim verified.

ex.main: **26,437 + 18,725 = 45,162.** The two pieces rebuild the start, so the difference is right.
ex.tip: The near-miss options are off by one or scramble the digits — the check only counts if every digit agrees.

questions.q: A concert sells 61,500 tickets and 45,987 people have arrived. How many are still to come?
steps: Ones: 0 − 7 — trade: 10 − 7 = 3. Tens: after lending, the 0 borrows too: 9 − 8 = 1.
Hundreds: 4 − 9 — trade: 14 − 9 = 5. Thousands: 0 after lending — borrow: 10 − 5 = 5.
Ten thousands: 5 − 4 = 1. Still to come: 15,513.

ex.main: **15,513.** Borrows rippled across four columns — exactly the terrain where the check matters.
ex.tip: Ticket-counter problems are subtraction saying "how far apart are these two numbers" — the gap picture again.

questions.q: Subtracting 82,354 − 47,182, in which place does the FIRST regroup happen?
opts: The tens — 5 tens cannot give up 8 tens
questions.hint: Scan right to left for the first top digit that is too small.
steps: Ones: 4 − 2 works, no trade.
Tens: 5 − 8 cannot go — first trade, right here.
For the record, the thousands will also borrow (2 under 7), and the difference is 35,172.

ex.main: **The tens.** Scouting the columns before working them tells you the whole shape of the problem.
ex.tip: This scan takes five seconds and removes every surprise from the algorithm. Make it a ritual.

questions.q: Dev computes 43,512 − 19,268 and gets 36,356. His check: 36,356 + 19,268 = 55,624, which is not 43,512. What should Dev do with that information?
opts: Trust the check — the answer is wrong; he flipped every short column, and the true difference is 24,244
Trust his first answer — checks sometimes fail
Round the check until it matches
Split the difference between the two numbers
questions.hint: The check cannot lie. What kind of error makes an answer too BIG?
steps: The check failed by a lot, so the subtraction is wrong — that part is settled.
His answer is bigger than a sensible estimate (44,000 − 19,000 = 25,000), which points at flipped columns.
Flipping short columns steals from the answer's neighbours and inflates it: 36,356.

ex.main: **The check has spoken — redo it; 24,244 is the truth.** A failed check is not a suggestion.
ex.tip: The estimate flagged it too — 36,356 is eleven thousand past 25,000. Two alarms, same fire.

questions.q: A puzzle: ▲ − 21,893 = 12,394. What is ▲, and how do you find it?
opts: 34,287 — add the two known pieces; subtraction run backwards is addition
12,394 — the difference is always the start
It cannot be found without more information
questions.hint: The start was split into two known pieces. Rebuild it.
steps: ▲ was cut into two pieces: the 21,893 removed and the 12,394 left.
Rebuild the whole: 21,893 + 12,394 = 34,287.
Confirm forwards: 34,287 − 21,893 = 12,394.
Solving backwards is just the check, promoted to the main event.

ex.main: **34,287, by adding the pieces.** Every subtraction fact hides an addition fact, and this puzzle asks for it.
ex.tip: Forward: predict the difference. Backward: recover the start. Owning both directions is what mastery means here.

questions.q: Estimating 61,234 − 29,876 as 61,000 − 30,000 = 31,000: is the exact answer above or below 31,000?
opts: Above — rounding pushed the start down AND the amount subtracted up, so the estimate dug too deep both ways
questions.hint: Track each rounding separately: which way did each one push?
steps: 61,234 → 61,000: the start shrank by 234, pushing the result down.
29,876 → 30,000: the amount removed grew by 124, pushing the result down again.
Both pushes point the same way, so the estimate must sit BELOW the truth.
Exact: 31,358 — above 31,000, as promised.

ex.main: **Above.** When both roundings push the same direction, the estimate stops guessing and starts promising.
ex.tip: This is 2-2's over/under reasoning applied to subtraction — the logic transfers, with the directions flipped for the subtrahend.
